title: What is hypertension?
text: Hypertension, or high blood pressure, is a chronic medical condition where the blood pressure in the arteries is persistently elevated. Blood pressure is expressed by two measurements: systolic (when the heart contracts) and diastolic (when the heart relaxes). A normal reading is around 120/80 mmHg. Hypertension is generally diagnosed when readings consistently exceed 130/80 mmHg. It is a major risk factor for heart disease, stroke, kidney failure, and other serious health problems. Most people with hypertension experience no symptoms, which is why it is often called the silent killer. Lifestyle changes such as reducing sodium intake, regular exercise, maintaining a healthy weight, and limiting alcohol can help manage blood pressure. Medications including ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, and diuretics may also be prescribed.

title: What are the symptoms of type 2 diabetes?
text: Type 2 diabetes is a chronic condition that affects how the body processes blood sugar (glucose). Common symptoms include increased thirst, frequent urination, increased hunger, unintended weight loss, fatigue, blurred vision, slow-healing sores, frequent infections, and areas of darkened skin (typically in the armpits and neck). Symptoms often develop slowly and may go unnoticed for years. Risk factors include obesity, sedentary lifestyle, family history, age over 45, and certain ethnic backgrounds. Diagnosis is typically made through fasting blood glucose tests, A1C tests, or oral glucose tolerance tests. Management involves lifestyle changes, monitoring blood sugar, and medications such as metformin or insulin in advanced cases.

title: How does the influenza vaccine work?
text: The influenza vaccine, commonly known as the flu shot, helps protect against the influenza virus. It works by introducing inactivated or weakened forms of flu viruses, or specific viral proteins, into the body. This stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies against the virus without causing illness. If a vaccinated person is later exposed to the actual flu virus, their immune system can recognize and fight it more effectively. The vaccine is updated annually to match the strains predicted to be most prevalent that flu season. The CDC recommends annual flu vaccination for everyone aged 6 months and older, with rare exceptions. Common side effects include soreness at the injection site, mild fever, and muscle aches, which typically resolve within a day or two.

title: What is asthma and how is it treated?
text: Asthma is a chronic respiratory condition in which the airways narrow, swell, and produce extra mucus, making breathing difficult and triggering coughing, wheezing, and shortness of breath. Asthma can be triggered by allergens (pollen, dust mites, pet dander), respiratory infections, cold air, exercise, stress, and air pollution. Treatment typically involves two types of medications: long-term control medications such as inhaled corticosteroids that reduce airway inflammation, and quick-relief inhalers such as albuterol that provide rapid symptom relief. An asthma action plan, developed with a healthcare provider, helps patients monitor symptoms and respond to flare-ups. Severe asthma attacks require immediate medical attention and may need emergency treatment with oxygen, nebulizers, or systemic corticosteroids.

title: What causes migraines?
text: Migraines are a neurological condition characterized by intense, debilitating headaches, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light and sound. The exact cause is not fully understood but involves changes in the brainstem and its interactions with the trigeminal nerve, as well as imbalances in brain chemicals such as serotonin. Common triggers include hormonal changes (especially in women), certain foods (aged cheeses, processed meats), food additives (MSG, aspartame), drinks (alcohol, caffeine), stress, sensory stimuli (bright lights, strong smells), changes in sleep, physical exertion, weather changes, and certain medications. Treatment options include pain-relieving medications taken during attacks (triptans, NSAIDs) and preventive medications taken regularly to reduce frequency and severity (beta-blockers, antidepressants, anti-seizure drugs, CGRP inhibitors).

title: What is the difference between bacterial and viral infections?
text: Bacterial infections are caused by bacteria, single-celled microorganisms that can live in many different environments. Viral infections are caused by viruses, which are smaller than bacteria and require a host cell to reproduce. Examples of bacterial infections include strep throat, urinary tract infections, and tuberculosis. Examples of viral infections include the common cold, influenza, COVID-19, and HIV. Bacterial infections are often treated with antibiotics, which kill bacteria or stop their growth. However, antibiotics are completely ineffective against viral infections, and overuse contributes to antibiotic resistance. Viral infections may be treated with antiviral medications in some cases, but many resolve on their own with supportive care. Vaccines exist to prevent many viral infections. Proper diagnosis often requires laboratory tests because symptoms can be similar.

title: How can I manage stress effectively?
text: Effective stress management involves a combination of lifestyle changes, coping strategies, and sometimes professional support. Regular physical exercise reduces stress hormones and stimulates the production of endorphins. Mindfulness practices such as meditation, deep breathing exercises, and yoga can calm the mind and reduce anxiety. Maintaining a healthy diet, getting adequate sleep (7-9 hours for adults), and limiting caffeine and alcohol also help. Time management techniques, setting realistic goals, and learning to say no can prevent overwhelm. Social support from friends, family, or support groups is crucial. Hobbies and recreational activities provide important mental breaks. If stress becomes chronic or unmanageable, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and other forms of counseling can be highly effective. In some cases, healthcare providers may prescribe medications for anxiety or depression related to chronic stress.

title: What are the warning signs of a stroke?
text: A stroke is a medical emergency that occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is interrupted. The acronym FAST helps recognize the warning signs: F for Face drooping (one side of the face droops or feels numb), A for Arm weakness (one arm is weak or numb, drifts downward when raised), S for Speech difficulty (slurred speech, inability to speak, or difficulty understanding), and T for Time to call emergency services immediately. Other warning signs include sudden numbness or weakness in the face, arm, or leg (especially on one side); sudden confusion or trouble speaking; sudden trouble seeing in one or both eyes; sudden trouble walking, dizziness, or loss of balance; and sudden severe headache with no known cause. Time is critical because brain cells die quickly without oxygen. Treatment within 3-4.5 hours of symptom onset can dramatically improve outcomes. Even if symptoms resolve quickly (transient ischemic attack), immediate medical attention is essential.

title: What is a balanced diet?
text: A balanced diet provides the body with all the essential nutrients it needs to function properly, in appropriate proportions. It includes a variety of foods from all major food groups: fruits and vegetables (at least 5 servings per day for vitamins, minerals, and fiber), whole grains (such as brown rice, oats, and whole wheat for sustained energy and fiber), lean proteins (such as fish, poultry, beans, and legumes for tissue repair and growth), dairy or dairy alternatives (for calcium and vitamin D), and healthy fats (such as those from olive oil, nuts, and avocados). It is also important to limit added sugars, saturated and trans fats, and sodium. Hydration with water is essential, with most adults needing 8 cups (2 liters) per day. Portion sizes should match individual energy needs based on age, sex, activity level, and health goals. A balanced diet supports immune function, energy levels, weight management, and reduces the risk of chronic diseases.

title: What is COVID-19 and how does it spread?
text: COVID-19 is a respiratory illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, first identified in late 2019. The virus spreads primarily through respiratory droplets and aerosols when an infected person coughs, sneezes, talks, or breathes. It can also spread through close contact and, less commonly, by touching contaminated surfaces and then touching the face. Symptoms range from mild (fever, cough, fatigue, loss of taste or smell, body aches) to severe (difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain, confusion). Some people remain asymptomatic but can still transmit the virus. Risk factors for severe disease include older age, obesity, diabetes, heart disease, lung disease, and immunocompromised states. Prevention measures include vaccination, wearing masks in high-risk settings, hand hygiene, ventilation, and avoiding crowded indoor spaces during outbreaks. Treatment ranges from supportive care for mild cases to antiviral medications (such as Paxlovid) and hospitalization with oxygen therapy or mechanical ventilation for severe cases.

title: How much sleep do adults need?
text: Most adults need 7 to 9 hours of quality sleep per night for optimal physical and mental health. Sleep needs vary slightly by individual but rarely fall below 6 or exceed 10 hours for healthy adults. Quality sleep involves moving through multiple sleep cycles, including REM (rapid eye movement) and deep sleep stages, which are essential for memory consolidation, immune function, and emotional regulation. Chronic sleep deprivation is linked to increased risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity, depression, weakened immunity, and impaired cognitive function. Sleep hygiene practices that promote good sleep include maintaining a consistent sleep schedule, creating a dark and cool bedroom environment, avoiding screens for at least an hour before bed, limiting caffeine after noon, avoiding large meals and alcohol close to bedtime, and incorporating relaxation techniques. If sleep problems persist despite good sleep hygiene, consult a healthcare provider to rule out conditions like sleep apnea, insomnia, or restless leg syndrome.

title: What is the recommended daily water intake?
text: General guidelines recommend that adults consume about 8 cups (2 liters or 64 ounces) of water per day, though individual needs vary. The U.S. National Academies of Sciences suggests an adequate daily fluid intake of about 3.7 liters (125 ounces) for men and 2.7 liters (91 ounces) for women, including water from beverages and food (about 20 percent of fluid intake comes from food). Water needs increase with hot weather, physical activity, illness with fever or vomiting, pregnancy, and breastfeeding. Signs of adequate hydration include pale yellow urine, infrequent thirst, and normal energy levels. Dehydration symptoms include dark yellow urine, dry mouth, fatigue, dizziness, and confusion. Severe dehydration is a medical emergency. While water is the best choice, other fluids like herbal teas, milk, and water-rich foods (cucumbers, watermelon, oranges) also contribute to hydration. Excessive water intake (over 4-6 liters in a short time) can be dangerous, leading to hyponatremia.

title: What are common side effects of antibiotics?
text: Common side effects of antibiotics include digestive issues such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain, often caused by disruption of the natural gut microbiome. Some people experience yeast infections (oral thrush or vaginal yeast infections) as antibiotics can disrupt the balance of bacteria and yeast in the body. Allergic reactions range from mild rashes and hives to severe reactions like anaphylaxis, which is a medical emergency. Penicillins and cephalosporins are common culprits for allergic reactions. Photosensitivity (increased sensitivity to sunlight) can occur with certain antibiotics like tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones. Other potential side effects include headaches, dizziness, and changes in taste. Long-term or repeated antibiotic use can contribute to antibiotic resistance, a growing global health concern. Probiotics may help restore gut flora during and after antibiotic treatment. Always complete the full prescribed course of antibiotics, even if symptoms improve, to prevent resistance and ensure complete eradication of the infection.

title: What is depression and how is it treated?
text: Depression, clinically known as major depressive disorder, is a common but serious mental health condition characterized by persistent feelings of sadness, hopelessness, and loss of interest in activities once enjoyed. Symptoms include changes in appetite and weight, sleep disturbances (insomnia or excessive sleeping), fatigue, difficulty concentrating, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, physical symptoms like aches and pains, and recurrent thoughts of death or suicide. To be diagnosed with depression, symptoms must persist for at least two weeks. Causes are multifactorial, involving genetics, brain chemistry, hormones, life events, trauma, and chronic illness. Treatment is typically most effective when it combines psychotherapy (especially cognitive behavioral therapy or interpersonal therapy) and medication (such as SSRIs, SNRIs, or other antidepressants). Lifestyle changes including regular exercise, adequate sleep, social connection, and stress management also play important roles. Severe cases may require additional interventions such as electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) or transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). If you or someone you know has thoughts of suicide, seek immediate help by calling a crisis hotline or emergency services.

title: What should I do for a sprained ankle?
text: A sprained ankle occurs when the ligaments that support the ankle are stretched or torn, usually from rolling, twisting, or turning the ankle awkwardly. The standard initial treatment follows the RICE protocol: Rest the ankle by avoiding activities that cause pain or swelling; Ice the area for 15-20 minutes every 2-3 hours during the first 48 hours to reduce swelling; Compression with an elastic bandage helps reduce swelling but should not be too tight; Elevation of the ankle above heart level when possible reduces swelling. Over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen or acetaminophen can help with pain and inflammation. Most mild sprains heal within 1-3 weeks with proper care. Seek medical attention if you cannot bear weight on the ankle, if there is severe pain or significant swelling, if the ankle appears deformed, if there is numbness, or if symptoms do not improve within a few days. Severe sprains may require imaging studies (X-rays or MRI), immobilization with a brace or boot, and physical therapy to restore strength, balance, and range of motion.
